Thus spoke my prophetic soul, as, torn by remorse, horror, and despair, I beheld those I loved spend vain sorrow upon the graves of William and Justine, the first hapless victims to my unhallowed arts.

To my intense surprise, there was no one with him. He was quite alone, and on the table opposite him was what I knew at once from the description to be a phonograph. I had never seen one, and was much interested.

Toad eagerly scrambled into the seat vacated by the driver, took the steering-wheel in his hands, listened with affected humility to the instructions given him, and set the car in motion, but very slowly and carefully at first, for he was determined to be prudent.
notes: Source: The Wind in the Willows, Kenneth Grahame

notes: Source: The Great Gatsby, F. Scott Fitzgerald

We both sat in silence for some little time after listening to this extraordinary narrative. Then Sherlock Holmes pulled down from the shelf one of the ponderous commonplace books in which he placed his cuttings.

notes: Source: Little Women, Louisa May Alcott

text: With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bitts and fasces of harpoons for spurs, would I could mount that whale and leap the topmost skies, to see whether the fabled heavens with all their countless tents really lie encamped beyond my mortal sight!

A Venus flytrap can count. The trap only snaps shut when an insect touches two trigger hairs within about twenty seconds, and it starts digesting only after several more touches. This prevents it from wasting energy on false alarms.

A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun, but it lasts only a fraction of a second. In that brief instant, it can carry a current of over two hundred thousand amperes.

A cheetah accelerates from zero to sixty miles per hour in about three seconds, quicker than most sports cars. But it can hold its top speed for only about twenty seconds before overheating forces it to give up the chase.

A cloud weighing over a million pounds floats because the tiny water droplets that form it are spread across a massive volume. Each individual droplet is so small that the slightest updraft of warm air keeps it suspended.

A colony of ants can collectively carry objects fifty times their combined body weight. Their strength comes from their tiny size, which gives them a favourable strength-to-weight ratio, and from their remarkable coordination.

A flea can jump roughly a hundred fifty times its own body length. If humans could do the same, we would be able to leap over skyscrapers. Fleas achieve this through a spring-like mechanism in their legs.

A giraffe's neck contains the same number of vertebrae as yours: just seven. Each one is simply enormous. To pump blood all the way up to its brain, a giraffe needs blood pressure roughly twice as high as a human's.

A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance. These birds get their pink colour from the carotenoid pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat. In captivity, without that diet, they gradually turn white.

A hummingbird's heart beats more than twelve hundred times per minute during flight. To fuel that engine, the bird must eat roughly half its body weight in nectar every single day. At night, some enter a deep torpor to conserve energy.

A jiffy is an actual unit of time. In physics, it refers to the time it takes light to travel one centimetre, which is roughly thirty-three point three trillionths of a second. The word has been in scientific use since the early twentieth century.

A jumping spider has eight eyes and vision sharper than a cat's, packed into a body smaller than a fingernail. Some species can even see colors that are invisible to humans, including light in the ultraviolet range.

A single bolt of lightning contains enough energy to toast about a hundred thousand slices of bread. The temperature of a lightning bolt can reach thirty thousand degrees, which is five times hotter than the surface of the sun.

A single lightning bolt can heat the air around it to temperatures five times hotter than the surface of the sun. This sudden heating causes the air to expand explosively, creating the sound wave we hear as thunder.

A single strand of spider silk is thinner than a human hair, yet pound for pound it is stronger than steel. If you could make a rope from spider silk as thick as a pencil, it could stop a fighter jet in flight.

A sneeze leaves your body at up to a hundred miles per hour and can launch droplets far across a room. It is also nearly impossible to sneeze with your eyes open, thanks to an involuntary reflex that clamps them shut.
A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about six billion tons on Earth. Neutron stars are so dense that their gravity compresses all their mass into a sphere only about twelve miles across.

About a third of people never develop wisdom teeth at all. As human jaws shrank over evolutionary time, the third molars became more trouble than they were worth. Dentists expect them to grow rarer with each passing millennium.

About six million years ago, the Mediterranean Sea dried up almost completely, leaving a mile-deep salt desert. When the Atlantic finally broke through at Gibraltar, the basin may have refilled in the largest flood in our planet's history.

Ancient Roman concrete actually gets stronger with age. Seawater reacts with the volcanic ash in the mixture, growing new crystals that seal cracks as they form. Modern engineers are still trying to fully copy the recipe.

Antarctica is the driest continent on Earth. Parts of it have not received rain in over two million years. Surprisingly, it is classified as a desert because it receives so little annual precipitation.

Astronauts return from space up to two inches taller. Without gravity compressing the spine, the discs between the vertebrae expand. The extra height disappears within a few months back on Earth, often accompanied by considerable back pain.

At the end of an Apollo mission, an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather side by side on the moon. With no air resistance, they hit the ground together, confirming Galileo's centuries-old prediction in front of a television audience.

Baobab trees can store tens of thousands of gallons of water in their swollen trunks. Some individuals in Africa are estimated to be over two thousand years old. Locals call them upside-down trees because their branches look like roots.
Butterflies taste with their feet. When they land on a plant, sensors on their legs detect chemicals to determine whether the surface is suitable for laying eggs or worth investigating for nectar.

Camel humps do not store water. They store fat, which the animal converts to energy and moisture when food is scarce. A thirsty camel can drink as much as thirty gallons of water in about fifteen minutes.

Cats spend roughly seventy percent of their lives sleeping. A fifteen-year-old cat has been awake for only about five years of its life. Scientists believe this sleep pattern evolved to conserve energy for short bursts of hunting.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The pyramids were already over two thousand years old by the time she was born.

Coffee is the second most traded commodity on Earth, right behind crude oil. Over two billion cups are consumed every single day. The global supply chain that delivers your morning cup is staggeringly complex.

Crows can recognize individual human faces and hold grudges for years. Researchers wearing specific masks found that crows would scold them long after a single negative encounter, even passing the knowledge to their offspring.

Days on Earth are gradually getting longer. The moon's gravity acts as a brake on our planet's rotation, adding about two milliseconds per century. Back when the dinosaurs lived, a full day lasted roughly twenty-three hours.

Dragonflies are arguably the deadliest hunters on Earth. They catch about ninety-five percent of the prey they target, compared to roughly fifty percent for lions. Their secret is a brain that predicts exactly where the prey will be.

During your lifetime, you will spend roughly two weeks waiting for traffic lights to change. That figure comes from averaging the daily time spent at red lights over a typical driving career of several decades.

Elephants communicate using rumbles pitched too low for humans to hear. These infrasonic calls travel for miles through the ground, and other elephants detect them through their feet. A herd can coordinate its movements across vast distances this way.

Email is older than the web by about two decades. The first message between two machines was sent in nineteen seventy-one, and its sender later admitted he could not remember what it said, guessing something like the top row of the keyboard.

Every time you shuffle a standard deck of fifty-two cards, the order you create has almost certainly never existed before and will almost certainly never exist again. The number of possible arrangements exceeds the number of atoms on Earth.

Every year, the Sahara Desert sends millions of tons of dust across the Atlantic Ocean to the Amazon rainforest. This dust carries phosphorus, a nutrient critical for plant growth, essentially fertilizing the jungle from thousands of miles away.

Fingernails grow about three to four times faster than toenails. Nails on your dominant hand grow slightly faster too, and growth speeds up in summer. Scientists think blood flow and daily micro-trauma from typing drive the difference.

Glass is not a slow-moving liquid, despite what you may have heard. That common myth comes from old cathedral windows being thicker at the bottom. The real reason is that medieval glassmaking techniques produced uneven panes.

Golf has been played on the moon. In nineteen seventy-one, astronaut Alan Shepard smuggled a club head aboard Apollo Fourteen and hit two balls. In the weak lunar gravity, he joked that the second one flew for miles and miles.

Here is something most people get wrong about goldfish. They do not actually have a three-second memory. Studies show they can remember things for months, and they can even be trained to push levers and navigate mazes.

Homing pigeons can find their way back from places they have never seen, hundreds of miles away. They appear to navigate using the Earth's magnetic field, the position of the sun, and even familiar smells and landmarks.

Honey bees can fly at speeds up to fifteen miles per hour and visit between fifty and a hundred flowers during one collection trip. A single bee produces only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its entire lifetime.

Horses can sleep standing up thanks to a system of tendons and ligaments that locks their legs in place. They only lie down for deep sleep, and in a herd, some horses stand guard while the others rest.

Humans share about sixty percent of their DNA with bananas. While that sounds surprising, it simply reflects the fact that all living things on Earth share a common ancestor and many of the same fundamental biological processes.

In nineteen thirty-two, Australia declared war on emus. Soldiers with machine guns were deployed to stop the birds from destroying wheat crops. The emus scattered, regrouped, and largely outmaneuvered the military, and the operation was quietly abandoned.

In parts of Southeast Asia, thousands of fireflies flash in perfect unison, lighting entire riverbanks like blinking holiday displays. Scientists studied the synchrony for decades, and the underlying math now helps explain heart cells and power grids.

In the eighteen thirties, ketchup was sold as medicine. An Ohio physician claimed his tomato pills could cure indigestion and rheumatism. The fad collapsed within a decade, but tomato ketchup survived and went on to conquer the condiment aisle.

Japanese honeybees have a remarkable defense against giant hornets. Hundreds of bees swarm the intruder in a tight ball and vibrate their flight muscles, cooking the hornet alive with heat that the bees themselves can barely survive.

Light from the sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. That means when you look at a sunset, you are actually seeing the sun as it was eight minutes in the past. Every sunrise is a glimpse of recent history.

Lobsters were once considered food for the poor. In colonial America, they were so plentiful that they washed ashore in piles and were fed to prisoners and servants. Their status as a delicacy did not emerge until the mid-eighteen hundreds.

Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive more than a century after her death. They are stored in lead-lined boxes in a Paris library, and researchers who wish to read them must sign a waiver and wear protective gear.

More people have been to the moon than have reached the deepest point of the ocean. Twelve astronauts walked on the lunar surface, while only three people have descended to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

Most diamonds form about a hundred miles below the Earth's surface under extreme heat and pressure. They are carried to the surface by volcanic eruptions that create narrow pipes of a special rock called kimberlite.

Mount Everest grows about four millimeters taller every year as the Indian tectonic plate continues to grind into Asia. The same slow collision that raised the entire Himalayan range is still happening beneath the mountain right now.

Mount Everest is not actually the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from base to peak. That title goes to Mauna Kea in Hawaii, which rises over thirty-three thousand feet from the ocean floor, with most of it hidden underwater.

Napoleon was not actually short. At five foot seven, he was average height for a Frenchman of his era. The myth came from British propaganda and from confusion between French and English units of measurement.

No one has ever seen eels breed in the wild. European eels travel thousands of miles to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, yet scientists have never observed the act itself. Their life cycle remained a complete mystery for centuries.

Olympic gold medals are mostly silver. The rules require only about six grams of actual gold, applied as plating over a solid silver core. The last Olympic medals made of solid gold were awarded back in nineteen twelve.

On Neptune and Uranus, it may literally rain diamonds. Extreme pressure deep in their atmospheres can squeeze carbon into diamond crystals that sink toward the core. Laboratory experiments have recreated the process here on Earth.

One tablespoon of soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on the planet. A healthy handful of garden soil may hold billions of bacteria, fungi, and other microscopic life forms that drive essential nutrient cycles.

Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. Teaching at Oxford began around ten ninety-six, while the Aztec civilization was not founded until thirteen twenty-five. The university predates the empire by over two centuries.

Painting the Golden Gate Bridge is a job that never ends. Crews continuously touch up its famous International Orange coating to fight salt-air corrosion. The color itself was originally just a primer that the architect decided to keep.

Peanuts are not actually nuts. They are legumes, cousins of peas and lentils, and they grow underground rather than on trees. After its flowers are pollinated, the peanut plant literally pushes its seed pods down into the soil.

Pineapples take about two years to grow. A single plant produces just one fruit per harvest cycle. That long growing time, combined with the difficulty of large-scale farming, is part of why they were once considered a luxury item.
Polar bear fur is not actually white. Each strand is hollow and transparent, scattering visible light in a way that makes the bear appear white. Underneath their fur, polar bears have jet-black skin.

Raindrops are not actually teardrop-shaped. Small ones are nearly perfect spheres, while larger ones flatten out into something closer to a hamburger bun shape. Air resistance on the bottom causes that flattening effect.

Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that would float in water. Despite being enormous, it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, giving it a density lower than water itself. You would need a very large bathtub, of course.

Scientists recently discovered that trees in a forest communicate through an underground network of fungi. They share nutrients, send distress signals, and even recognize their own offspring. Some researchers call it the wood wide web.

Scotland's national animal is the unicorn. It has held that title since the twelfth century. In Celtic mythology, the unicorn symbolized purity, innocence, and power, qualities the Scots wanted to represent.

Ships crossing the Panama Canal are lifted eighty-five feet above sea level and then lowered back down on the other side, like climbing a staircase of water. Each transit uses roughly fifty million gallons of fresh water.

Some cicadas emerge only once every thirteen or seventeen years, and those numbers are no accident. Both are prime numbers, which makes it much harder for predators with shorter life cycles to sync their generations to the feast.

Termite mounds are marvels of natural air conditioning. Their intricate tunnel networks circulate air and keep the interior temperature stable within a degree or two, even when the outside swings by fifty. Architects have copied the design for office buildings.

The Amazon River once flowed in the opposite direction. Millions of years ago, it emptied into the Pacific Ocean rather than the Atlantic. The rise of the Andes Mountains gradually reversed its course.

The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, which makes the water so dense that you float without trying. Its surface sits more than fourteen hundred feet below sea level, the lowest dry land on Earth.

The Eiffel Tower grows by about six inches every summer. The iron structure expands in the heat and contracts again in the winter. Engineers accounted for this thermal expansion when they built it in eighteen eighty-nine.

The Empire State Building went up in just four hundred ten days, an average of four and a half floors per week. More than three thousand workers swarmed the site, racing to claim the title of the world's tallest building.

The Great Wall of China is not actually visible from space with the naked eye. That is one of the most persistent myths in popular culture. Astronauts have confirmed this repeatedly since the earliest space missions.

The London Underground has been slowly baking the clay around it for over a century. The tunnels were pleasantly cool when they opened in eighteen sixty-three, but decades of train heat have warmed the surrounding earth by more than ten degrees.

The Pacific Ocean is so large that it contains its own antipodal point. In other words, you could draw a straight line through the centre of the Earth from one side of the Pacific and come out still in the Pacific on the other side.

The Pantheon in Rome still holds the record for the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, nearly nineteen hundred years after it was built. Its builders lightened the concrete toward the top and left an open hole at the center.

The Sahara was green only a few thousand years ago. Cave paintings deep in the desert show people swimming, herding cattle, and fishing in lakes. Slow changes in Earth's orbit shifted the monsoon and dried the region out.

The Slinky was born when a naval engineer knocked a spring off a shelf and watched it walk down a stack of books. More than three hundred million have been sold, and the toy has even flown aboard the space shuttle.

The Wright brothers' first powered flight covered just a hundred twenty feet, a distance shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet. Within sixty-six years of that moment, human beings were walking on the moon.

The appendix may not be useless after all. Recent research suggests it serves as a safe house for beneficial gut bacteria, repopulating the digestive system after illness. Species with an appendix have evolved one independently more than thirty times.
The average person produces enough saliva in their lifetime to fill two swimming pools. Saliva plays a crucial role in digestion, wound healing, and protecting your teeth from bacterial decay.

The average person spends about six months of their life waiting in lines. That figure comes from a study that tallied the time spent queuing at shops, banks, airports, and government offices over a typical adult lifetime.

The axolotl can regrow entire limbs, parts of its heart, and even sections of its brain. Unlike other salamanders, it never fully grows up, keeping its feathery gills and its aquatic lifestyle for its entire life.

The brain itself cannot feel pain. It has no pain receptors of its own, which is why surgeons can operate on a fully awake patient. Headaches actually come from nerves, blood vessels, and muscles in the surrounding tissue.

The claim that no two snowflakes are alike is probably true. A single snowflake contains around a quintillion water molecules, and the number of possible arrangements is so astronomically vast that exact duplicates are effectively impossible.

The continents drift at about the same speed your fingernails grow. The Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly an inch every year, which means it is about fifteen feet wider today than when Columbus sailed across it.

The deepest point in the ocean is the Mariana Trench, nearly seven miles below the surface. At that depth, the water pressure is over a thousand times what you feel at sea level. Yet life still thrives there.

The dot over the lowercase letters i and j has a name. It is called a tittle. The word comes from the Latin titulus, meaning a small distinguishing mark. It has been used in English typography since the Middle Ages.

The first computer bug was an actual insect. In nineteen forty-seven, engineers found a moth trapped in a relay of the Harvard Mark Two computer. They taped it into the logbook with a note recording the first real case of a bug.

The first computer programmer was born in eighteen fifteen. Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for a mechanical computer that was never even built, and she predicted that machines might one day compose music. It took a century for technology to catch up.

The first oranges were not orange. The original fruit from Southeast Asia was green. The orange colour we know today was developed through selective breeding over centuries, mainly in warmer Mediterranean climates.

The human eye can distinguish approximately ten million different colours. However, the exact number varies between individuals. Some people, called tetrachromats, have a fourth type of cone cell and can see even more.
The human nose can detect over one trillion distinct scents. For a long time, scientists believed the number was closer to ten thousand. Recent research has completely overturned that old estimate.
The inventor of the Pringles can, Fredric Baur, was so proud of his creation that when he died in two thousand eight, his family buried part of his ashes inside one.

The inventor of the fire hydrant is unknown because the patent was destroyed in a fire. The irony has made this one of the most frequently cited pieces of trivia, though some historians dispute whether it is entirely accurate.

The largest tree on Earth by volume is a giant sequoia named General Sherman. It weighs an estimated two point seven million pounds and is still growing. Every year it adds enough wood to make an ordinary sixty-foot tree.

The largest volcano in the solar system is on Mars. Olympus Mons stands nearly three times the height of Mount Everest and covers an area the size of Arizona. Its slopes are so gradual you could walk up without noticing.
The longest English word that can be typed using only the top row of a standard keyboard is typewriter. Whether this was intentional on the part of the keyboard's designer remains a matter of debate.

The longest hiccuping spree ever recorded lasted sixty-eight years. Charles Osborne of Iowa started hiccuping in nineteen twenty-two and did not stop until nineteen ninety. He hiccuped approximately four hundred thirty million times.

The longest place name still in use belongs to a hill in New Zealand. It has eighty-five letters and roughly translates to the place where a man played his flute for his beloved. Most locals just call it Taumata Hill.

The longest recorded flight of a chicken lasted thirteen seconds. Chickens can fly short distances and reach speeds of about ten miles per hour, but their heavy bodies and short wings make sustained flight impossible.

The marathon's odd distance of twenty-six point two miles exists because of British royalty. The nineteen oh eight London course was extended so the race could start beneath the windows of Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box.

The monarch butterflies that fly south to Mexico each autumn have never been there before. The journey spans multiple generations, yet each new wave returns to the same forests, and sometimes the very same trees, as their great-grandparents.

The most precise atomic clocks would lose less than a second over the entire age of the universe. They are so sensitive that raising one just a few inches changes how fast it ticks, because gravity runs clocks at different rates.

The narwhal's tusk is actually a tooth that grows in a spiral through its upper lip, sometimes reaching ten feet long. It is packed with millions of nerve endings, and scientists believe it senses temperature and salinity.

The original name for the search engine Google was BackRub. Larry Page and Sergey Brin changed the name in nineteen ninety-seven. The word Google is a play on googol, which is the number one followed by a hundred zeros.

The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on the planet. In a hunting dive, it can exceed two hundred forty miles per hour. Special baffles in its nostrils let it breathe at speeds that would burst other birds' lungs.

The shortest commercial flight in the world takes about ninety seconds. It connects the islands of Westray and Papa Westray in Scotland, covering a distance of only one point seven miles across the water.

The sound you hear when you crack your knuckles is not bones rubbing together. It is actually the sound of gas bubbles collapsing in the fluid between your joints. Despite popular belief, it does not cause arthritis.
The tallest building in the world, the Burj Khalifa, is so tall that you can watch the sunset from the ground floor and then ride the elevator to the top and watch it set a second time.

The temperature at the centre of the Earth is roughly the same as the temperature on the surface of the sun. This intense heat comes from residual energy left over from the planet's formation and from radioactive decay deep inside the core.

The total computing power used to send astronauts to the moon in nineteen sixty-nine was less than what is found in a modern pocket calculator. The Apollo guidance computer had roughly sixty-four kilobytes of memory.
The total length of all the blood vessels in your body is roughly sixty thousand miles. That is enough to circle the Earth more than twice. Most of that length comes from the tiniest capillaries.

The world's first website is still online. Tim Berners-Lee published it in nineteen ninety-one to explain what the World Wide Web was and how to use it. You can still visit the page today at its original address.

The world's largest flower smells like rotting flesh on purpose. The corpse flower's stench attracts the flies and beetles that pollinate it. It blooms only once every several years, and each event draws crowds to botanical gardens.

There are more possible combinations in a Rubik's Cube than seconds that have passed since the Big Bang. The cube has over forty-three quintillion permutations, yet skilled solvers can find the solution in under four seconds.

There are more possible iterations of a chess game than there are atoms in the observable universe. The number of legal board positions alone exceeds ten to the forty-seventh power, a truly incomprehensible figure.

There is a species of jellyfish that is effectively immortal. When the Turritopsis dohrnii is injured or stressed, it can revert its cells back to their youngest form and start its life cycle all over again.

Venice stands on millions of wooden piles driven into the mud more than a thousand years ago. Deprived of oxygen underwater, the wood never rotted. Instead, minerals slowly hardened it into an almost stone-like foundation.

Viking sailors may have navigated cloudy seas using crystals called sunstones. Certain minerals split light in a way that reveals the sun's position even when it is hidden. Medieval texts mention the stones, and one was found in a shipwreck.

Voyager One is the most distant human-made object, over fifteen billion miles from Earth. Its radio signals, traveling at the speed of light, take more than twenty-two hours to arrive. It still phones home nearly every day.

When Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii, it preserved the city in astonishing detail. Archaeologists have found loaves of bread still sitting in ovens, complete with the baker's stamp. The eruption froze a single ordinary morning for two thousand years.

When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance. The angle of the dance encodes the direction relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle encodes the distance.

When the first platypus specimen reached Europe, scientists thought it was a hoax. A venomous, egg-laying mammal with a duck bill seemed impossible. It also hunts with its eyes closed, sensing electric fields through its bill.

White chocolate contains no cocoa solids, which is why purists insist it is not really chocolate. It is made from cocoa butter, sugar, and milk. The cocoa butter carries the aroma of chocolate without any of the color or bitterness.

Wombat droppings are cube-shaped. Scientists believe this helps the droppings stay in place on rocks and logs, which wombats use to mark their territory. The shape is produced by the varying elasticity of their intestinal walls.

Yawns really are contagious. Seeing, hearing, or even reading about yawning can trigger one. The effect is stronger between people who know each other well, and dogs can catch yawns from their owners too.

You cannot tickle yourself. Your cerebellum predicts the sensations your own movements will cause and cancels the response before it starts. Researchers use this quirk to study how the brain tells self from other.

Young sunflowers track the sun across the sky from east to west, then swing back overnight to face the dawn. Once mature, they stop moving and permanently face east, because morning warmth attracts more pollinators to the blooms.

Your body contains about thirty-seven trillion cells. Each one carries a complete copy of your DNA, which, if stretched out end to end from a single cell, would extend about six feet. Lined up from every cell, the total length would reach the sun and back several hundred times.

Your body literally glows. Humans emit a faint visible light produced by chemical reactions inside our cells, about a thousand times weaker than our eyes can detect. The glow is brightest in late afternoon and dimmest late at night.

Your bones are about five times stronger than steel of the same weight. A cubic inch of bone can bear a load of roughly nineteen thousand pounds before it fails. This remarkable strength comes from a composite structure of collagen and minerals.

Your brain uses about twenty percent of your total energy, even though it makes up only two percent of your body weight. When you are thinking hard, your brain does not actually use much more energy than when you are daydreaming.

Your liver can regrow to full size from as little as a quarter of its original tissue. It is the only human organ with this ability, and a living donor's liver typically regenerates within just a few months.

Your stomach lining replaces itself every three to four days. If it did not, the strong acid inside would digest the stomach itself. This constant renewal is one of the fastest cell turnover rates in the human body.

Your taste buds live for only about ten days before being replaced. That is why a burned tongue recovers so quickly. As we age, the replacement cycle slows down, which is partly why flavors seem stronger in childhood.
